The rapid proliferation of DERs can outpace planned grid reinforcement, creating a trade-off between enabling local energy resilience and the technical strain on underprepared utility infrastructure. Working with local power providers is key to transparency for DOW. 2.6 Radar Disruption Wind turbines’ large size and rotating blades reflect electromagnetic waves, creating interference that reduces radar sensitivity and hinders its ability to accurately track targets (DOE n.d.; WTRIMWG 2025). Radar systems can detect fast-moving blades as objects, complicating the identification and tracking of airborne targets and disrupting critical weather forecasting (WTRIMWG 2025). Radars can be tuned to reduce the detection of “noise” caused by wind turbines, but the false positives that wind turbines create could complicate DOW’s detection of small, low-flying drones and increase the likelihood of missed or misidentified targets (DOE 2024). The potential for maritime radar interference will increase as offshore wind plants proliferate (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2022). In 2024, Sweden canceled plans for 13 offshore wind plants in the Baltic Sea, in part citing concerns that the turbines’ interference with sensors and radars would hinder the detection of submarines and potential adversary attacks (Bryant 2024). Working with foreign partners and frequent updates of methodologies to filter out such interference can mitigate this risk. 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3 Drivers of Adoption Risk Drivers of adoption-related risks occur due to the adoption of advanced energy technologies. 3.1 Breadth of Available Technologies The sheer volume of available technologies and the uncertainty surrounding global adoption and infrastructure build-out present challenges for DOW to prioritize investments and select technologies for different applications and environments, increasing the complexity of defense acquisition processes and possibly leading to the adoption of subpar technologies. With different units adopting different solutions for tactical, operational, and strategic energy needs, DOW might struggle to streamline the vast number of potential energy solutions. Spreading capital investment too thin could divert resources away from improving or maintaining existing energy infrastructure, complicating strategic decision-making in energy resource allocation (Simulcik, Villalobos, and Bazilian 2025). Additionally, without an explicit plan for deployment to areas with appropriate infrastructure, the acquisitions system risks acquiring legacy assets with extended lifespans that might become increasingly difficult or costly to maintain. For example, in 2024, DOW acquired approximately 17,600 internal combustion engine vehicles and 2,900 electric vehicles (EVs) (U.S. GSA 2024), and these vehicles will require ongoing maintenance and parts throughout their lifespans. In 2023, the average federally owned military vehicle was 12.4 years old (U.S. GSA 2024). An integrated DOW cross-service approach to working with government laboratories and commercial developers to determine which emerging technologies best suit DOW needs should improve clarity on technology choices. 3.2 New Logistics Requirements Advanced energy technologies present risks and uncertainties related to weight, size, safety, and ease of assembly and disassembly. Advanced energy systems have varied sets of logistics demands, and the military adoption of these technologies will require updating protocols, including servicing, storage, transportation, and disposal (Lutton 2024).
